title: State (BSES YPL) v. Gaffar Miya
court: Addl. Sessions Judge-05 (Electricity), East, Karkardooma Courts, Delhi
result: Convicted under Section 135, Electricity Act, 2003; civil liability (theft bill Rs. 55,332) settled and deposited during trial; posted for hearing on sentence
statutes: Third proviso to Section 135(1) Electricity Act 2003

interpretations.interpretation: Clause (a) — tapping or making a connection with a licensee's overhead, underground or service lines/wires — is the operative limb in a direct-hooking case (clauses (b)–(e) needing a metering/tampering foundation). 'Dishonestly' being undefined in the Act, Section 24 IPC supplies the definition (wrongful gain to one person or wrongful loss to another); drawing supply through an unmetered illegal Teflon-wire tap satisfies dishonest intention.

A reverse-onus clause: proof of an artificial or unauthorised means of abstraction raises a presumption of dishonest use 'until the contrary is proved'. 'Shall presume' is a compulsory presumption (Neeraj Dutt); the accused must adduce evidence making his defence reasonably probable to a prudent man (Hiten P. Dalal); the natural rebuttal is proof of a lawful, metered source, typically paid bills, the onus lying on the consumer under Section 106 Evidence Act (Mukesh Rastogi).

citations.case: Sonu @ Amar v. State of Haryana
citations.principle: Objection that an electronic record was admitted without a Section 65B certificate goes to the mode of proof and must be raised when the record is tendered; if not taken at trial it cannot be raised later.

citations.case: Balu Sudam Khalde v. State of Maharashtra
citations.principle: Incriminating suggestions put by defence counsel in cross-examination bind the accused and can establish facts such as the factum of, and presence at, the inspection.

citations.case: Punjab State Electricity Board v. Ashwani Kumar
citations.principle: An inspection report prepared by officers in discharge of official duty carries a presumption of regularity; onus on the consumer to rebut by cogent evidence.

citations.case: Sushil Sharma v. BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd.
citations.principle: Non-examination of an independent/public witness is no infirmity where inspecting officials are trustworthy and bear no enmity to the accused.
'Shall presume' denotes a compulsory legal presumption the court is bound to draw until the fact is disproved.

citations.case: Hiten P. Dalal v. Bratindranath Banerjee
citations.principle: Rebuttal of a statutory presumption need not be conclusive; evidence must make the defence reasonably probable to a prudent man.

citations.case: Mukesh Rastogi v. North Delhi Power Ltd.
citations.principle: Easiest rebuttal of the theft presumption is production of paid electricity bills; Section 106 Evidence Act places that onus on the consumer.

significance.explanation: Absence of a 65B certificate for inspection videography is not fatal where the defence did not object when the electronic record was tendered — the objection goes to the mode of proof and is waived if not timely taken (Sonu @ Amar).

significance.point: Defence cross-examination can prove the case
significance.explanation: Incriminating suggestions put by defence counsel — here, that the wires ran from the ground-floor meter's input terminal — can themselves establish the factum of inspection and bind the accused (Balu Sudam Khalde).

significance.point: The reverse-onus presumption does real work
significance.explanation: Once an unauthorised means of abstraction is proved, the 'shall presume' clause compels a presumption of dishonest theft; the consumer must rebut with evidence of a lawful metered source — typically paid bills under the Section 106 onus (Mukesh Rastogi); a bare denial with no defence evidence will not suffice.

significance.point: A public witness is not essential
significance.explanation: Non-joining of an independent witness does not vitiate an otherwise trustworthy official inspection without shown enmity (Ashwani Kumar; Sushil Sharma).

significance.point: Settling the theft bill can cut against the accused
significance.explanation: Payment of the civil liability during trial was read not as closure but as conduct corroborating guilt on the criminal charge.

generic_facts.theft_mode: direct theft / hooking — no meter at premises; Teflon wires tapped from input terminal of ground-floor meter (meter for ground floor only)
generic_facts.premises: residential floor of a multi-storey house (2nd floor)
generic_facts.meter_status: no meter installed for inspected premises
generic_facts.occupant_at_inspection: lady claiming to be a tenant of the accused (Sitara)
key_evidence: seized Teflon wires produced in court
generic_facts.defence: bare denial and false implication; no defence evidence; settled theft bill during trial
